newsitem.title: INDIA: India parties eye poll as coalition cracks show.
newsitem.headline: India parties eye poll as coalition cracks show.

text.p: India's political parties have begun preparing for a mid-term election after a split in Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party that weakened his minority coalition, politicians and analysts said on Wednesday.
"Everybody is getting ready for elections," a cabinet minister in the 15-party United Front coalition, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters.

Gujral's Janata Dal (JD) party, which leads the coalition of centrists, regional groups and communists, was split last Saturday by its then-president Laloo Prasad Yadav, who formed a powerful breakaway group that named itself the Rashtriya (Nationalist) Janata Dal (RJD).
The next day his rival, Sharad Yadav -- no relative of his -- was declared elected as Janata Dal leader in polls held last Thursday.
Laloo Yadav, a popular low-caste leader mired in a corruption scandal, cited the alleged rigging of voter lists in the party poll as the reason for his ouster.
Despite the political turmoil, Gujral's two-month-old rule appeared secure.
Laloo Yadav, chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, immediately pledged the breakaway RJD's support to Gujral.
The RJD has taken 18 of the Janata Dal's 45 deputies.
"It is a fairly critical period for the government," said analyst Mahesh Rangarajan at the Centre for Contemporary Studies. "Any one thing can upset the apple cart."
But he said there was no immediate threat to the government. "It is vulnerable but not yet fragile," he said.
Trouble began on Tuesday when leftist coalition partners said they wanted RJD out of the United Front if Laloo Yadav did not resign as chief minister and face trial for corruption.

Yadav has been indicted by federal police in a $280 million corruption scandal in which he is among 56 politicians and officials accused of embezzling animal welfare funds in Bihar. But he says he is innocent and has rejected calls to quit.

Gujral has refused to sack three federal government ministers who joined the RJD, but his Janata Dal colleagues will continue to try to persuade the premier to force out the party renegades, the minister said.
Leftist parties led by the communists may quit the coalition if the RJD was allowed to stay on without Yadav resigning, the minister said.
"The types of statements they (leftists) are coming out with will further weaken the United Front," Food Minister Raghuvansh Prasad Singh, one of the three RJD ministers, told reporters.

The crucial factor for the government is the Congress party. Congress offers the make-or-break support of its 140 lawmakers to the United Front, which has 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house, the Lok Sabha, which was elected in April/May 1996.
"That (JD split) is an internal matter," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said on Wednesday. "There is no change in our stand. We continue to support the Gujral government."

Congress backed the United Front in June 1996 to oust a 12-day-old government formed by its arch foe, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janta Party (BJP), which is the largest group in parliament with 193 votes.

But Congress pulled its support in April and toppled the United Front government headed by then-prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, accusing him of failing to contain the BJP. The United Front changed leaders to win back Congress' support.
"I don't see a stable arrangement emerging in this house," Rangarajan said. "There will certainly be a mid-term poll."
